config.title: Permutations

intro.title: Permutations
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that generates all possible permutations of a given array of numbers. You will learn the core programming concept of backtracking, which explores all potential arrangements by building solutions incrementally and undoing choices when needed. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, recursion, and conditional logic. By the end, you will understand how to systematically generate permutations and implement this algorithm from scratch.
intro.usecase: Permutations are essential for generating all possible arrangements of items, which appears in many real-world software features. E-commerce sites use permutations to display different sorting options for product listings (price low-high, newest first, best rated). Travel booking platforms generate all possible flight or hotel combinations when users filter by multiple criteria. In content management systems, permutations help create all possible URL slug variations or tag combinations for SEO optimization. Developers implement permutation algorithms to build recommendation engines that suggest different product bundles or playlist orders based on user preferences.

objectives: Implement a recursive function to generate all permutations of an array
Construct a base case to terminate recursion when the permutation is complete
Manipulate arrays by swapping elements to explore different ordering possibilities
Initialize a results array to store and return all generated permutations
Apply backtracking to revert array state after exploring each permutation branch
Integrate array copying to preserve original permutations in the results collection
Configure the recursive function parameters to track current position and remaining elements

content.body: Have you ever tried to arrange a set of items in every possible order? That's what permutations are all about. Today we'll learn how to generate all permutations of an array using a powerful technique called backtracking.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain the backtracking approach to generating permutations
2. Implement a recursive function that builds permutations
3. Understand when and why we need to undo choices
4. Apply backtracking to solve similar combinatorial lessons
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple example. Suppose we have the array [1, 2, 3]. Try to list all possible orders you can arrange these three numbers. How many different arrangements can you find?
content.title: Try it

content.body: Think about how you built those arrangements. Did you start by picking 1, then 2, then 3? What if you picked 1, then 3, then 2? Notice that after picking 1 and 2, you had to 'go back' and try picking 3 instead of 2 to explore different branches.
content.title: Explore the process

content.body: What you just did was explore possibilities systematically. You made a choice, followed it to completion, then went back to try different choices. This is the essence of backtracking.
content.title: What you did

content.body: With 3 items, you could probably list all 6 permutations manually. But what if you had 5 items? That's 120 permutations! Or 10 items? That's over 3.6 million! We need a systematic way to generate all permutations without missing any.
content.title: Why it gets complex

content.body: Backtracking follows a simple pattern: try a choice, explore what happens, then undo if it doesn't lead to a solution (or when you're done exploring that path). For permutations, we try each available number, recursively build the rest, then undo our choice to try other options.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Explore a path; if it dead-ends, go back and try another branch.

content.body: We'll build permutations step by step using recursion. At each step, we pick an unused number, add it to our current permutation, then recursively build the rest. After exploring that choice, we remove it (undo) to try other numbers. This ensures we explore all possible arrangements.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Start with an empty current permutation and all numbers available
2. For each available number:
   - Add it to the current permutation
   - Mark it as used
   - Recursively build the rest of the permutation
   - Remove it from current permutation (undo)
   - Mark it as available again (undo)
3. When current permutation is complete, save it
4. Continue until all possibilities are explored
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called permute that takes an array nums as parameter. Initialize two empty arrays: result to store all permutations, and current to track the current permutation being built.
steps.hint: You'll need function permute(nums) with let result = [] and let current = [] inside.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function declaration with parameters and empty arrays initialized
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have both result and current arrays initialized.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to declare the function with nums parameter and initialize both arrays.

steps.title: Create helper function
steps.instruction: Inside permute, define a helper function called backtrack. It will handle the recursive building of permutations.
steps.hint: Add function backtrack() {} inside permute, after initializing result and current.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Define function backtrack() {} inside permute.
steps.feedbackWrong: You need to create a function called backtrack inside permute.

steps.title: Add base case
steps.instruction: In the backtrack function, add the base case: if current.length equals nums.length, we have a complete permutation. Push a copy of current to result and return.
steps.expectedOutcome: Base case that saves complete permutations
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! This handles when we've built a full permutation.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your condition: current.length should equal nums.length.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to check if current is complete, then save a copy to result.

steps.title: Loop through available numbers
steps.instruction: After the base case, add a for loop to iterate through nums. For each number, we'll check if it's already in current (skip if it is).
steps.hint: Use for (let num of nums) { if (current.includes(num)) continue; ... }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure you're checking if the number is already in current.
steps.feedbackWrong: You need a loop through nums and a check for used numbers.

steps.title: Try a choice
steps.instruction: Inside the loop (after the continue), add the current number to our permutation: current.push(num).
steps.hint: Add current.push(num); backtrack(); inside the loop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Remember to both add the number AND call backtrack().
steps.feedbackWrong: You need to push the number to current, then call backtrack recursively.

steps.title: make the recursive call: backtrack()
steps.hint: Add current.push(num); backtrack(); inside the loop.
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Undo the choice
steps.instruction: After the recursive call, we need to undo our choice to try other options. Add current.pop() to remove the last number we added.
steps.expectedOutcome: Removing the last number to backtrack
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You need to remove the last element from current.
steps.feedbackWrong: After exploring with a number, use current.pop() to undo that choice.

steps.title: Start and return
steps.instruction: Finally, call backtrack() to start the process, and return result at the end of permute.
steps.expectedOutcome: Complete function that returns all permutations
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Don't forget to call backtrack() and return result.
steps.feedbackWrong: You need to start the backtracking process and return the result.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented a backtracking algorithm to generate all permutations. Remember: backtracking follows the pattern of try → explore → undo. This pattern is powerful for solving many combinatorial lessons where you need to explore all possibilities. The key insight is that after exploring one path, you must undo your last choice to try other options.
content.title: Done
